CAPUT PRIMUM.
DECRETUM SYNODI.

Decretum Synodi sic se habet, vertente e Gallico in Latinum Sermonem D. Garissolio, in Ecclesia & Academia Montalbanensi Verbi Dei Ministro & SS. Theologiae Professore.

Cum relatum fuisset ad Synodum, scripta quaedam, alia typis evulgata, alia manu exarata, prodisse, quae totam rationem peccati originalis sola corruptione haereditaria in omnibus hominibus inhaerente definiunt, & primi peccati Adae imputationem negant: Damnavit Synodus doctrinam ejusmodi, quatenus peccati Originalis naturam ad corruptionem haereditariam posterorum Adae ita restringit, ut imputationem excludat primi illius peccati, quo lapsus est Adam: Adeoque censuris omnibus subjiciendos censuit Pastores, Professores, & quoscunque alios, qui in hujus quaestionis disceptatione a communi sententia recesserint Ecclesiarum Protestantium, quae omnes hactenus & Corruptionem illam, & Imputationem hanc in omnes Adami posteros descendentem agnoverunt. Sed & illud eadem Synodus omnibus Colloquiis & Synodis Provincialibus injungit, ut quos Theologiae candidatos ad sacrum ministerium evehendos curaverint, ii jubeantur huic Decreto Chirographum suum subscribere.

HOC Decretum etiam ab ipsis Synodis Provincialibus varie acceptum est. Quibusdam enim placuit illud executioni mandari: Aliis vero visum judicium suum sustinere, illiusque Decreti executionem usque ad alteram Synodum Nationalem suspendere. Fuere ex pastoribus & privatis hominibus, qui illud ut necessarium, ut aequissimum, ut verissimum exoscularentur: Non defuere contra, qui illud ut novum, ut non necessarium, ut nimis festinanter, re haud satis pensitata, Synodisque Provincialibus inconsultis factum, immo ut minus Dei verbo consentaneum rejicere auderent.
english: Chapter One. The decree of the Synod.

The decree of the Synod runs as follows, Antoine Garissoles — minister of the Word of God and professor of sacred theology in the church and academy of Montauban — turning it from French into Latin speech.

When it had been reported to the Synod that certain writings had come forth, some published in type, others drawn out by hand, which define the whole account of original sin by hereditary corruption alone inhering in all human beings, and deny the imputation of Adam's first sin: the Synod condemned doctrine of that sort, insofar as it so restricts the nature of original sin to the hereditary corruption of Adam's posterity that it excludes the imputation of that first sin by which Adam fell (Genesis 3:6). And therefore it judged that pastors, professors, and any others who, in the discussion of this question, have withdrawn from the common judgment of the Protestant churches — churches which have all hitherto acknowledged both that corruption and this imputation descending upon all Adam's posterity (Romans 5:12) — should be subjected to all censures. But the same Synod also enjoins upon all colloquies and provincial synods that those whom they cause to be advanced as candidates of theology to the sacred ministry are to be ordered to subscribe their own hand to this Decree.

This Decree has also been variously received by the provincial synods themselves. To some it seemed good that it be put into execution. To others it seemed right to hold their judgment in suspense, and to suspend the execution of that Decree until another National Synod. There were among pastors and private persons those who kissed it as necessary, as most equitable, as most true. There were not wanting, on the other side, those who dared to reject it as new, as not necessary, as made too hastily, the matter scarcely weighed enough, and without consulting the provincial synods — indeed, as less agreeable to the Word of God.

Interim rumor sparsus est per totam Galliam, isque etiam ad exteras nationes permanavit, eo Decreto damnatam fuisse Placei de imputatione primi Adae peccati sententiam, quem illi, qui animo erant Academiae Salmuriensi minus benevolo, avide arripuerunt, famamque Placei tanquam ἀνοσίου & a Synodo Nationali convicti & damnati, variis cum sermonibus tum scriptis, imo libris typis excusis, expressoque etiam in quibusdam ejus nomine, dilacerarunt. Unde natum est apud multos infirmos grave scandalum, & studiosorum SS. Theologiae ingens perturbatio, magnum vulnus Academiae Salmuriensi illatura, nisi Synodi quaedam Provinciales medicinam adhibuissent in tempore. Placeus enim sibi in hac causa fere defuit, nihilque praeter manuscriptum illud composuit, quod D. Garissolius Manuscriptum posterius appellavit. Nimirum bona conscientia & veritate, cujus Deus opportuno tempore vindex est, fretus, rem totam ejus providentiae, & Synodo Nationali proximae committendam putavit; hortantibusque amicis sese potius ad confutandos Socinianos, & divinam Domini nostri Iesu Christi essentiam demonstrandam convertit. Sed potuit mea quidem sententia utrumque facere, & pro divina Domini nostri natura propugnare, & famae suae Academiaeque Salmuriensi, praesertim apud exteras gentes, libello aliquo edito consulere; Ac, nisi fallor, debuit: potuit enim explicatione sententiae suae omnem ab ea reprehensionis maculam abstergere, conservata Decreti Synodici autoritate illibata: revera enim cum eo non pugnat, immo congruit magis quam eorum opinio, qui eam oppugnant; ac propterea ut videri posset & a Synodo damnata, & ab ipsis confutata, eam qui vel non intellexerunt vel intelligere noluerunt, adeo immutarunt, ut in oppositam transformaverint. Id quod nisi faciam luce meridiana clarius, non recuso quin pro mendace & calumniatore habear.

Cum igitur videam & Synodum Nationalem de anno in annum differri, cupientesque quasi fugere, civili bello quominus convocari possit jam ab aliquot annis obstante; & interim quibusdam in locis severius cum SS. Theologiae studiosis agi, & exteras gentes a libris Placei, tanquam ab haeretico autoritate Synodi nationalis damnato conscriptis, abhorrere, & permultos cognoscere quae sit Placei sententia vehementer cupere: putavi me consulturum veritati & gloriae Dei, aedificationi & paci Ecclesiae, honori Synodi Nationalis, famae Academiae Salmuriensis & Placaei, consolationi studiosorum Theologiae, necnon operis quod pro divinitate Domini nostri Placeus inchoavit, continuationi; si ostendero, nec damnatam esse a Synodo Placei de imputatione primi Adae peccati sententiam, nec eam talem esse, qualem hactenus plerique omnes sunt opinati. Ita, nisi vehementer fallor, omnis ista de imputatione peccati Adamici controversia, etiam antequam conveniat Synodus Nationalis, extinguetur, id quod a Domino nostro Iesu Christo, cujus ope fretus hoc opus aggredior, vehementer opto & spero.
english: Meanwhile a rumor was scattered through all France, and it even reached foreign nations, that by that Decree Placeus's judgment concerning the imputation of Adam's first sin had been condemned — a rumor which those less well disposed toward the Academy of Saumur seized eagerly, and tore Placeus's reputation to pieces as of an unholy man, convicted and condemned by the National Synod, with various speeches and writings, even books printed in type, and in some of them with his name expressly set down. Hence there arose among many of the weak a grave scandal, and among students of sacred theology a huge disturbance — a great wound that would have been dealt to the Academy of Saumur, had not certain provincial synods applied medicine in time. For Placeus almost failed himself in this cause, and composed nothing beyond that manuscript which Garissoles called the later Manuscript. Relying on a good conscience and on the truth, of which God is the vindicator in due time, he thought the whole matter should be committed to God's providence and to the next National Synod; and at his friends' urging he turned himself rather to confuting the Socinians and to demonstrating the divine essence of our Lord Jesus Christ. But in my judgment he could have done both — to contend for the divine nature of our Lord, and to look after his own reputation and that of the Academy of Saumur, especially among foreign peoples, by publishing some little book. And unless I am mistaken, he ought to have done so: for by explaining his own judgment he could have wiped every stain of reproach from it, while the authority of the Synodical Decree was kept intact. For in truth it does not fight with that Decree; rather it agrees with it more than does the opinion of those who attack it. And therefore, so that it might seem both condemned by the Synod and confuted by them, those who either did not understand it or refused to understand it so changed it that they transformed it into its opposite. Unless I make this clearer than noonday light, I do not refuse to be held a liar and a calumniator.

Since, then, I see both that the National Synod is put off from year to year, and that those who wish it almost flee it, civil war already for some years standing in the way of its being convened; and that meanwhile in certain places students of sacred theology are treated more severely, and foreign nations shrink from Placeus's books as from writings composed by a heretic condemned by the authority of the National Synod, and that very many intensely desire to know what Placeus's judgment is: I thought I would serve the truth and the glory of God, the edification and peace of the Church, the honor of the National Synod, the reputation of the Academy of Saumur and of Placeus, the consolation of students of theology, and also the continuation of the work Placeus began for the divinity of our Lord, if I should show that Placeus's judgment concerning the imputation of Adam's first sin was neither condemned by the Synod, nor is it such as nearly all have hitherto supposed. So, unless I am badly mistaken, this whole controversy about the imputation of Adam's sin will be extinguished even before a National Synod convenes — which I earnestly wish and hope from our Lord Jesus Christ, by whose help I undertake this work.

CAPUT II.
Eo Decreto non esse damnatam Placei sententiam septem argumentis probabilibus ostenditur.

Eo Decreto damnatam non esse Placei sententiam multis argumentis partim valde probabilibus, partim plane necessariis, probare possumus.

Primum enim de primi peccati, quo Adam lapsus est, imputatione nullum ante Synodum illam Nationalem scriptum a Placeo prodierat, praeter Theses de statu hominis lapsi ante gratiam disputatas publice mense Febr. An. 1640, quinquennio antequam illud Decretum fieret, eodemque anno ad eos omnes Pastores missas, qui in finitimis Provinciis librorum edendorum examini praefecti erant: atque etiam ipsi Synodo Pictonum, quae eodem anno Castroheraldi habita est, oblatas Placei nomine a Clariss. eius Collega D. Amyraldo ad eam Synodum ab Andium Provincia delegato. De illis autem Thesibus toto illo quinquennio nemo litem Placeo moverat, nemo eum accusaverat, neque causa ista ullo modo vel in Senatu Academiae, vel in Presbyterio Ecclesiae, vel in Andium Synodo, cui ipse subest, vel (quantum ante Synodum illam Nationalem rescire potuit) in ulla alia Synodo agitata fuerat. Itaque sub clypeo Art. XXXI. Cap. V. Disciplinae Ecclesiasticae, quam viginti septem Synodi nationales comprobaverant, necnon Decreti Synodi Nationalis Alenconii convocatae An. 1637, prohibentis eiusmodi de doctrina accusationes ad Nationalem immediate deferri, ac iubentis ante et admoneri eum qui accusandus videretur, et causam in ea Synodo Provinciali cui subiicitur cognosci et disceptari, securus dormiebat. Accusari enim se in Synodo Nationali non posse intelligebat, nisi violatis illis Decretis, quae apud omnes Pastores et Synodos Provinciales putabat sacro-sancta et inviolata esse debere. Cum igitur verisimile non sit tanta quemquam, praesertim Pastorem, cupiditate, ne dicam pruritu, Placeum, a quo nullo modo laesus fuerat, accusandi, ut maluerit sciens prudens tam veneranda Decreta violare quam ab accusando sibi temperare: verisimile etiam non est Placeum fuisse a quoquam accusatum, qui si non est accusatus, profecto damnatus non est.

Frustra quis reponat, Aliquando contingere, ut necessariis de causis ab ordine semel constituto discedere debeant qui ordinem posuerunt. Quinam enim ordinem illum posuerant? quinam Decreta illa condiderant? Synodi Nationales. Fuitne ergo Synodus Nationalis Placei accusatrix? Annon si accusatus est, aut ab aliqua Synodo Provinciali, aut ab aliquo Synodi Provincialis delegato accusatus est, neutro ordinis illius autore, utroque Synodi Nationalis autoritati et Decreto subiecto? Deinde qui ordinem posuerunt ab ordine semel prudenter constituto non discedunt nisi necessariis de causis. Quaenam igitur causae necessariae discedendi ab ordine tam sapienter instituto, et violandi Decreta tam aequa tamque necessaria fuerunt? frustra eas requiro. Nullae apparent. Forte succrescenti malo ita occurrendum fuit. Cui malo? Placei sententiae? In ea duo: id quod credit, et id quod non credit. Quicquid credit, idipsum quicunque non sunt Pelagiani aut Semipelagiani crediderunt semper. Quod non credit, id neque ulla publica autoritate firmatum est unquam, neque ab eo reiicitur, nisi quia novum est, et a Dei verbo, a Doctrina Ecclesiarum protestantium, a recta ratione alienum. Itaque ab ea reiectione nihil fuit metuendum mali.

Sed fac malum fuisse cui esset occurrendum. Num ei fuit ita occurrendum, ut violarentur illae leges, illa decreta, quibus Synodi Nationales sapientissime praescripserant, quomodo tali malo, si quando oriretur, esset occurrendum? Quid, quod praepostera illa occurrendi ratio magis ad malum illud augendum, quam ad tollendum, accommodata fuisset? Cum enim Deus sit Deus ordinis, et velit omnia fieri in Ecclesia secundum ordinem et decenter, accusatio fratris a fratre ordinem in Ecclesia Dei recte constitutum violans probabilius perturbationi alicui humanae quam Dei Spiritui ascribi potuisset, et quantas Placeo opportunitates querendi, ac sententiam suam defendendi et propagandae attulisset, si uti occasione voluisset?

Quaenam igitur tandem necessaria causa fuisset violandi ordinem tanta autoritate et sapientia positum? Respondebit forte aliquis, Exclusos fuisse per angustias temporis qui rem ad Synodum nationalem detulerunt, quominus positae constitutioni obtemperare possent. Scilicet per angustias quatuor aut quinque annorum non licuit accusatoribus expostulationes suas ad Synodum Andium deferre. Sed enim Septembri demum mense habita est in Occitania superiori ea Synodus, in qua primum expositum est hoc negotium, et vero proximo Decembri convocandus erat Charentonii nationalis conventus. Esto. At primo cur expectata est illa Synodus Provincialis Nationali proxima? Cur in praecedente aliqua expositum non est hoc negotium? Excusari non potest thesium Placei in ea provincia ignoratio. Nam et quinquennio ante, ut dixi, vulgatae fuerant, et missae ab ipso Placeo ad D. Delonum Ecclesiae Montalbanensis Pastorem. Cur igitur tandiu dilata est Thesium illarum accusatio, siquidem sunt accusatae? Deinde cur saltem toto illo trimestri, quod inter Provincialem illam Synodum et Nationalem interfluxit, scriptum non est ad Placeum, ut saltem aliqua ex parte ordini satisfaceret? Cur non est admonitus de errore? Cur ab eo petita non est clarior opinionis explicatio? Cur saltem de futura illa accusatione non est aliquid vel ad ipsum, vel ad Senatum Academicum, vel ad Ecclesiam Salmuriensem perscriptum aut aliqua alia ratione significatum? Potest enim sancte iurare se nihil quicquam de futura illa accusatione inaudivisse, nisi nescio quid ex incerto rumore; et quidem cum ferebatur Synodus nationalis aut iam soluta, aut mox solvenda. Nam neque antequam coiret, neque illa durante verbum ullum de futura illa accusatione a Synodi superioris Occitaniae delegatis aut ad ipsum Placeum, aut ad eius Collegas qui tum Salmurii erant, scriptum est. Quod quo pertinere potuisset, nisi ut Placeus absens, incautus, inscius accusaretur et opprimeretur? Id autem de Synodo illa Provinciali, deque eius legatis suspicari, nedum credere, nonne tibi, pie lector, religio est?
english: Chapter Two. That Placeus's judgment was not condemned by that Decree is shown by seven probable arguments.
That Placeus's judgment was not condemned by that Decree we can prove by many arguments, some of them highly probable, others plainly necessary.

First: before that National Synod no writing of Placeus on the imputation of the first sin by which Adam fell had come out, except the Theses on the state of fallen man before grace, disputed publicly in February 1640 — five years before that Decree was made — and sent the same year to all those pastors who in the neighboring provinces were charged with examining books for publication; and also offered, in Placeus's name, by his most distinguished colleague Amyraut, Anjou's delegate, to the Synod of Poitou held that same year at Châtellerault. Through that whole five years no one had stirred a suit against Placeus over those Theses, no one had accused him, nor had the cause been agitated in any way in the Academy's Senate, or in the church's session, or in the Synod of Anjou to which he himself belongs, or (so far as he could learn before that National Synod) in any other synod. So under the shield of Art. XXXI, Cap. V of the Ecclesiastical Discipline — which twenty-seven national synods had confirmed — and of the Decree of the National Synod of Alençon convened in 1637, which forbids accusations of that kind about doctrine to be carried straight to a National Synod, and orders that the man who seems to need accusing be first admonished, and that the cause be heard and debated in the provincial synod to which he is subject, he slept secure. For he understood that he could not be accused in a National Synod unless those Decrees were violated — Decrees he thought every pastor and provincial synod ought to hold sacrosanct and inviolable. Since, then, it is not likely that anyone, least of all a pastor, would have such a craving — not to say itch — to accuse Placeus (who had never injured him) that he would knowingly and deliberately rather violate such venerable Decrees than keep himself from accusing: it is also not likely that Placeus was accused by anyone; and if he was not accused, he was certainly not condemned.

Someone will object in vain that those who once set an order must sometimes, for necessary causes, depart from the order once constituted. Who, then, had set that order? Who had made those Decrees? National Synods. Was the National Synod itself, then, Placeus's accuser? Or if he was accused, was he not accused either by some provincial synod, or by some delegate of a provincial synod — neither of them the author of that order, both of them subject to the National Synod's authority and Decrees? Next: those who set an order do not leave an order once wisely constituted except for necessary causes. What necessary causes, then, were there for leaving an order so wisely instituted, and for violating Decrees so equitable and so necessary? I look for them in vain. None appear. Perhaps a growing evil had to be met that way. What evil? Placeus's opinion? In it there are two things: what he believes, and what he does not believe. Whatever he believes, everyone who is not a Pelagian or Semi-Pelagian has always believed. What he does not believe has never been established by any public authority, and he rejects it only because it is new, and alien to the Word of God, to the doctrine of the Protestant churches, and to right reason. So nothing evil was to be feared from that rejection.

But grant that there was an evil that had to be met. Did it have to be met by violating those laws and decrees by which National Synods had most wisely prescribed how such an evil, if it ever arose, should be met? What is more: would not that upside-down way of meeting it have been better fitted to increase the evil than to remove it? For since God is a God of order, and wills that everything in the church be done according to order and decently, an accusation of a brother by a brother that violates the order rightly constituted in the church of God could more probably have been ascribed to some human disturbance than to the Spirit of God — and how many opportunities would it have given Placeus to complain, and to defend and spread his opinion, if he had chosen to use the occasion?

What necessary cause, then, could there finally have been for violating an order set with so much authority and wisdom? Someone will perhaps answer that those who brought the matter to the National Synod were shut out by the narrowness of time from being able to obey the constitution once laid down. As if, through the "narrowness" of four or five years, the accusers could not carry their complaints to the Synod of Anjou! But that Synod in Upper Occitania at which this business was first laid out was held only in September, and the national assembly at Charenton was to be convened the following December. Be it so. Yet first: why was that provincial synod nearest the National waited for? Why was this business not laid out in some earlier one? Ignorance of Placeus's theses in that province cannot be excused. For five years earlier, as I said, they had been published, and sent by Placeus himself to Delon, pastor of the church of Montauban. Why, then, was the accusation of those theses so long delayed, if indeed they were accused? Next: why at least through that whole trimester between that provincial synod and the National was nothing written to Placeus, so that he might at least in some measure satisfy the order? Why was he not admonished of error? Why was a clearer explanation of his opinion not asked of him? Why at least was nothing about that coming accusation written to him, or to the Academic Senate, or to the church of Saumur, or made known in some other way? For he can swear in good faith that he had heard nothing whatever of that coming accusation, except I know not what from an uncertain rumor — and that when the National Synod was already said to be dissolved, or about to be dissolved. For neither before it met, nor while it sat, was a single word about that coming accusation written by the delegates of the Upper Occitania Synod either to Placeus himself or to his colleagues then at Saumur. To what could that have tended, except that Placeus, absent, unwarned, and unaware, might be accused and crushed? And is it not a matter of conscience for you, pious reader, even to suspect — much less to believe — that of that provincial synod and of its delegates?

Huic argumento aliud non minus probabile subnectam. Si Placeus apud Synodum nationalem accusatus fuisset, nonne Synodus eum ad se vocari et citari curavisset? Quis enim eam voluisse credat pastorem, professorem Theologiae, integrae eatenus famae, viventem, absentem, inauditum, nec prius citatum, aut saltem de accusatione admonitum, damnare, cum magno multorum infirmorum scandalo, ac ministerii ipsius, necnon Academiae cui inseruit damno? Atqui eum Synodus illa nullo modo, neque directe, neque indirecte citavit aut citari curavit, cum tamen id per ordinarium tabellarium qualibet septimana bis terve fieri facillime posset.

Reponet forte aliquis, nihil opus citatione fuisse, quoniam non personae in discrimen, sed doctrinae duntaxat ad examen vocabantur. Quid audio? Non vocabatur in discrimen pastoris et professoris Theologiae fama, quae ipsi debet esse ipsa vita carior? Non vocabatur in discrimen eius ministerium, cuius efficacitati obesse nihil magis potest, quam si erroris momentosi in causa religionis damnatus a Synodo Nationali existimetur? Non subiiciebatur eius persona censuris omnibus, si quidem eo decreto eius doctrina damnabatur? Non iudicabatur pastoris et professoris Theologiae munere privandus, si quidem eo decreto studiosi Theologiae ob eius errorem a sacro verbi Dei ministerio excludebantur?

Dicet forte etiam aliquis, adfuisse inter omnes eximium, doctrina percelebrem et eloquentia, Placei Collegam, qui eius, quam ipse, sententiam multo melius et eloquentius apud Synodum defenderet. Aderat is quidem, eiusque dotes Placeus et admiratur et colit, et in parte felicitatis suae ponit talem habere Collegam. Sed neque cum eo de quaestione illa contulerat unquam, neque aliam ab eo in Synodo defensionem sperabat, nisi ut, si accusaretur, intercederet, quominus absens et inauditus condemnaretur. Quare si Placei causam suscepit apud Synodum orandam, id praeter Placei mentem evenit, eiusque in collegam benevolentiae ascribendum est, neque Synodum impedire debuit, quominus ipsum Placeum, si quidem nominatim accusabatur, citaret. Is enim, cum eiusmodi accusationem ordini in Ecclesia constituto repugnantem divinare, a nemine admonitus, non posset, neque sibi in Synodum veniendum putaverat, neque alium rogandum, ut pro se respondere, causamque suam apud Synodum tueri vellet. Porro si eius causam Clarissimus Collega suscepit, cur coactus est defensor accusatoris loco, hoc est, primo verba facere? Cur deinde postquam accusator dixit, respondere obiectaque argumenta et testimonia diluere defensori permissum non est? Quis unquam audivit rei accusati advocatum (si tamen advocatus dicendus est qui, reo inscio et accusationis prorsus ignaro, causam eius suscipit) priorem orare debere, postquam autem accusator oravit, respondere non debere?

Attamen ille solita subtilitate, solitaque sermonis splendore coram venerando Consessu suam et Placei causam plus bihorio egit. Suamne egerit necne, ipse viderit. Placei certe causa tantillo spatio agi non potuit. Potest enim pro sua causa tot argumenta, tot testimonia afferre, ut eis leviter attingendis, nedum explicandis et ab exceptionibus vindicandis bihorium vix possit sufficere. Immo nescit an vel unum argumentum possit tam brevi tempore, uti par est, expendi ac diiudicari. Solet enim ipse in uno argumento examinando non raro plures horas, immo dies ponere, sua ipsius experientia edoctus quod primo aspectu, aut levi adhibito examine verum apparet, nonnunquam tandem accuratius inspectum falsum esse cognosci.
english: To this argument I will add another no less probable. If Placeus had been accused before the National Synod, would the Synod not have had him summoned and cited to appear? Who would believe it willing to condemn a living pastor and professor of theology, of unblemished reputation until then, absent, unheard, not previously cited or even warned of the accusation — with great scandal to many of the weak, and harm to his ministry and to the Academy he served? Yet that Synod cited him in no way, neither directly nor indirectly, though the ordinary post could easily have done it two or three times any week.

Someone will perhaps reply that there was no need of a citation, because it was not the person that was put in danger, but only the doctrine that was called to examination. What do I hear? Was not a pastor and theology professor's reputation put in danger — a reputation that ought to be dearer to him than life itself? Was not his ministry put in danger — a ministry whose effectiveness nothing can injure more than the rumor that a National Synod has condemned him for a serious error in religion? Was not his person subjected to every censure, if that decree condemned his doctrine? Was he not judged worthy to be stripped of the pastoral and professorial office, if that decree shut theology students out of the sacred ministry of the Word because of his error?

Someone may also say that among those present there was an outstanding colleague of Placeus, famous for learning and eloquence, who could defend Placeus's judgment before the Synod far better and more eloquently than Placeus himself. That colleague was indeed present; Placeus both admires and honors his gifts, and counts it part of his own happiness to have such a colleague. But Placeus had never conferred with him on that question, and hoped for no other defense from him in the Synod than that, if Placeus were accused, he would intercede so that Placeus would not be condemned absent and unheard. So if he took up Placeus's cause to plead before the Synod, that happened beyond Placeus's intention, and is to be credited to kindness toward a colleague; and it ought not to have kept the Synod from citing Placeus himself, if he was being accused by name. For Placeus, never warned, could not have guessed at an accusation so contrary to the church's settled order; he had neither thought he must come to the Synod nor asked anyone else to answer and defend his cause there. Further: if his most distinguished colleague did take up his cause, why was the defender forced to speak first, in the accuser's place? Why, after the accuser had spoken, was the defender not allowed to answer and clear away the objections, arguments, and testimonies? Who ever heard that the advocate of an accused man (if he can even be called an advocate who takes up the cause of a defendant wholly unaware of the charge) must plead first, and after the accuser has pleaded must not reply?

And yet with his usual subtlety and his usual splendor of speech that colleague pleaded his own and Placeus's cause before the venerable assembly for more than two hours. Whether he pleaded his own cause or not, let him see. Placeus's cause, at least, could not be handled in so little time. For in his own cause he can bring forward so many arguments and testimonies that two hours could scarcely suffice even to touch them lightly, much less to unfold them and fence them from exceptions. Indeed he does not know whether even one argument can be weighed and judged in so short a time as fairness requires. For he himself, in examining a single argument, not rarely spends several hours — even days — taught by his own experience that what seems true at first glance, or on a light examination, is sometimes found false when inspected more carefully.

source_text:
Sed pergamus, tertiumque addamus argumentum. Nonne Theses Placei, si accusatae apud Synodum Nationalem fuissent, ei Synodo exhiberi, eaque audiente legi, et rationes omnes quibus opinionem suam Placeus brevissime quidem, sed tamen, ut ipse putat, invicte probavit, sigillatim et diligenter expendi debuissent? Atqui id in ea Synodo factum non esse certissimum est. Non sit igitur verisimile, fuisse, aut accusatas illas theses, aut saltem ita accusatas ut sint damnatae. Enimvero cur damnatae fuissent Theses quae fortiter communes adversarios oppugnabant, vel expugnabant potius, Socinum, Pelagium, Pighium, cum separatim thesibus primis quindecim, tum coniunctim sequentibus?

Succurrit etiam argumentum quartum. Nam si Synodus damnare Placei opinionem suo illo Decreto voluisset, num illa, qua erat prudentia, locis Scripturae et argumentis, seu numerum, seu robur spectes haudquaquam contemnendis, quibus ille suam opinionem confirmaverat, contenta fuisset nudum Protestantium consensum, quasi oblita Art. V. Confessionis fidei, quam suo calculo ipsa recens comprobaverat, opponere, et tanquam regulam fidei ac fundamentum suo illi Decreto substernere? Hoc mihi quidem certe non sit verisimile.

Sed neque mihi etiam verisimile videtur, Synodum prudentissimam, inconsultis Synodis Provincialibus una sessione definire voluisse controversiam momentoasam, in nulla unquam alia Synodo antea agitatam aut decisam. Id enim cum experientia periculosum esse docuit, tum abhorret a consuetudine Synodorum nationalium, quae de rebus longe minoris momenti pronunciare tutum saepe non censuerunt, nisi consultis prius omnibus provinciis: adeo vereri solent, ne vel potestate sua abutantur, vel ea cum cuiusquam infirmi scandalo minus circumspecte utantur. Attamen id fecit, si Placei sententiam suo illo decreto damnavit. Nam neque provincias consuluit, et una Sessione res confecta est, et ea peccati Adamici imputatio, quam Placeus thesibus suis reiecerat (non enim omnem reiecerat) nulla unquam Synodo, nulla unquam publica autoritate fuerat firmata. Quis igitur credat sapientissimam Synodum talem imputationem tanta cum festinatione definire voluisse, atque ad eam credendam et docendam omnes Synodos Provinciales, omnia colloquia, omnes Pastores et Professores, omnes sacri Ministerii candidatos, omnium censurarum metu inciso obligare?
english: But let us go on, and add a third argument. If Placeus's Theses had been accused before the National Synod, should they not have been laid before that Synod, read in its hearing, and all the reasons by which Placeus — briefly, to be sure, but still, as he thinks, invincibly — proved his opinion weighed one by one and carefully? Yet it is entirely certain that was not done in that Synod. So it is not likely that those theses were accused, or at least so accused that they were condemned. Why, after all, would theses have been condemned that vigorously attacked — or rather stormed — the common adversaries, Socinus, Pelagius, and Pighius, both separately in the first fifteen theses and jointly in those that follow?

A fourth argument also comes to hand. For if the Synod had meant to condemn Placeus's opinion by that Decree of theirs, would it — with the prudence it had — have been content to set against the Scripture texts and arguments (contemptible neither in number nor in strength) by which he had confirmed his opinion a bare consensus of Protestants, as if forgetful of Article V of the Confession of Faith which it had itself lately approved by its own vote, and to lay that consensus under its Decree as a rule of faith and a foundation? That, to me at least, is certainly not likely.

Nor does it seem likely to me that a most prudent Synod, without consulting the provincial synods, would have wished to settle in a single session a weighty controversy never before agitated or decided in any other synod. Experience has taught that to be dangerous; and it is also foreign to the custom of national synods, which have often judged it unsafe to pronounce even on matters of far less moment unless all the provinces had first been consulted — so careful are they not to abuse their power, or to use it without circumspection to any weak person's scandal. Yet that is what it did, if it condemned Placeus's judgment by that decree. For it neither consulted the provinces, and the business was finished in one Session, and that imputation of Adam's sin which Placeus had rejected in his theses (for he had not rejected every imputation) had never been established by any synod or by any public authority. Who, then, would believe that a most wise Synod would have wished to define such an imputation with so much haste, and to bind every provincial synod, every colloquy, every pastor and professor, and every candidate for the sacred ministry to believe and teach it, under threat of all censures?

source_text:
An etiam ille ipse qui Placeum accusasset, accusatoris partes strenue egisset oratione praemeditata, magno apparatu, multa eloquentia, magna vehementia, calens adhuc ab illa accusatione, ac sanguine commoto, nulla responsione, nulla mora interposita, iudex in illa causa sedisset, praesesque sententias rogasset? Num id passura fuisset aequissima Synodus, si in eo iudicio de doctrina, de fama Pastoris et professoris Theologiae actum fuisset, praesertim absentis, nec citati, nec ulla unquam censura notati? Id certe non est verisimile.

Multum abest Placeus ut probet, vel imitari velit morositatem Remonstrantium coram Synodo Nationali respondere detrectantium, magnamque ex ea partem delegatorum submoveri postulantium. Nam si etiam apud infensissimos iudices ratio fidei nostrae reddi potest et debet, et ab ipso Christo, eiusque Apostolis et martyribus reddita est, quanto magis apud Synodum ex fratribus constantem ac legitima magistratus autoritate convocatam reddi potest et debet? Si qui Remonstrantes antea accusaverant, aut sententiam suam declaraverant, illi censendi erant sumpta delegatorum ad Synodum Nationalem persona, atque religione iurisiurandi interposita, affectus et praeiudicia posuisse. Illud vero urget Placeus, quod est ab illa ipsa Synodo Dordracena sancte affirmatum: Neminem posse in eodem iudicio eiusdemque causae defensorem pariter et iudicem esse.

An etiam illa prudentissima Synodus Placeum, si quidem eum erroris momentosi damnandum voluisset, sivisset, ut antea, et SS. Ministerio in Ecclesia, et S. Theologiae professione in Academia Salmuriensi fungi, nulla adhibita vel ob praeteritum censura, vel in futurum cautione? Non curavisset eum ab aliquo Pastore de errore privatim aut publice admoneri, ut ab eo, si fieri posset, revocaretur? Non iussisset saltem Andium Synodum cum reo agere, ne pergeret turbare Ecclesiam Dei? An etiam putasset Synodus sua unius autoritate metienda esse Religionis dogmata, et adducta a Placeo Scripturae loca et argumenta praeponderari? Absit ut de ea id credamus, quod in Ecclesia Romana, ut tyrannicum, ab omnibus Protestantibus iure damnatur. Ipse sibi Placeus indignus videretur qui pro reformato haberetur, si pluris faceret unius Synodi nudam autoritatem quam Scripturam et deprompta ex Scriptura argumenta, quamdiu ei apparent insolubilia. Dedisset igitur certe operam Synodus, ut ab aliquo, cum argumenta Placei solverentur, tum ea, quibus mota Synodus Placei sententiam damnavisset, exponerentur, ut et iudicii sui aequitas pateret, et conscientias patefactione veritatis potius persuadere quam fide imperata videretur. Quandoquidem igitur nemo eorum qui Synodo illi interfuerunt, nemo eorum iussu vel hortatu ullum cum Placeo verbum sive viva voce, sive scripto habuit, quo eum a sententia dimoveret, aut eius argumenta dilueret, aut contraria iis diceret: eo satis aperte significatum est non esse Decreto illo Synodali Placeum damnatum.

Huc accedit quod Placei nomen abest a Decreto. Cur, si Placei nominatim accusati doctrina damnabatur? Aut enim damnasse Placei sententiam Synodus videri voluit, aut noluit. Si voluit: cur eius nomen non expressit? Si noluit, a Synodi mente illi abeunt, quibus eam damnasse videtur.
english: Would the very man who had accused Placeus — having played the accuser's part vigorously with a prepared speech, great apparatus, much eloquence, and great vehemence, still hot from that accusation and with his blood stirred — also, with no reply and no delay interposed, have sat as judge in that cause and, as moderator, have called for the votes? Would a most equitable Synod have allowed that, if in that trial the issue was a pastor and theology professor's doctrine and reputation — especially one absent, not cited, and never marked by any censure? That is certainly not likely.

Placeus is far from approving, or wishing to imitate, the peevishness of the Remonstrants who refused to answer before a National Synod and demanded that a large part of the delegates be removed on that account. For if the reason of our faith can and ought to be given even before the most hostile judges, and was given by Christ himself and by his apostles and martyrs, how much more can and ought it to be given before a Synod composed of brothers and convened by the lawful authority of the magistrate? If some Remonstrants had previously accused, or had declared their own judgment, they were to be counted, once they had taken the role of delegates to the National Synod and interposed the religion of an oath, as having laid aside affections and prejudices. What Placeus does urge is what that very Synod of Dort solemnly affirmed: that no one can be both defender and judge in the same trial of the same cause.

Would that most prudent Synod, if it had indeed meant Placeus to be condemned for a serious error, also have allowed him, as before, to serve both in the sacred ministry in the church and in the professorship of sacred theology in the Academy of Saumur, with neither censure for the past nor caution for the future? Would it not have arranged for some pastor to admonish him of the error privately or publicly, so that he might, if possible, be called back from it? Would it not at least have ordered the Synod of Anjou to deal with the accused, so that he would not go on troubling the church of God? Would the Synod also have thought that the dogmas of religion were to be measured by its authority alone, and that the Scripture texts and arguments Placeus brought forward were outweighed by it? Far be it from us to believe of that Synod what is rightly condemned in the Roman church by all Protestants as tyrannical. Placeus would think himself unworthy to be counted Reformed if he prized one synod's bare authority above Scripture and the arguments drawn from Scripture, so long as those still seemed insoluble to him. The Synod would therefore certainly have taken care that someone both answer Placeus's arguments and set out those by which the Synod, moved by them, had condemned his judgment — so that both the equity of its decision would be plain, and it would seem to persuade consciences by laying truth open rather than by commanding faith. Since, then, no one who took part in that Synod, and no one at their order or urging, exchanged any word with Placeus, orally or in writing, by which to move him from his judgment, or to dilute his arguments, or to state the contrary: by that it is shown clearly enough that Placeus was not condemned by that synodical Decree.

To this is added that Placeus's name is absent from the Decree. Why, if the doctrine of Placeus, accused by name, was being condemned? For either the Synod wished to seem to have condemned Placeus's judgment, or it did not. If it did: why did it not express his name? If it did not: those for whom it seems to have condemned him depart from the Synod's mind.

source_text:
CAPUT III. Idem probatur argumentis necessariis.

Superiora argumenta, ut ego arbitror, valde probabilia fuerunt; sequuntur necessaria. Primum enim qui damnari sententia Placei in ea Synodo potuit, in qua non est proposita vel exposita? Atqui non est in illa Synodo nationali exposita quae fecit illud decretum. A quo enim fuisset exposita, nisi ab eo, a quo fuisset accusata? Si quis autem eam accusavit apud Synodum, is fuit D. Garissolius Synodi illius praeses. Is autem quomodo eam uti est exponere tunc potuisset, qui, ne quidem quadriennio post, eam qualis est proponere potuit? Certe in sua Decreti Synodici explicatione et defensione is Placeo sententiam tribuit, quam Placeus non agnoscit, quaeque cum illis verbis aperte pugnat quibus mentem suam Placeus exposuerat cum datis ad eum literis, tum in eo manuscripto quod ei posterius appellare placuit, ut suo loco faciam sole meridiano clarius.

Ad hoc argumentum aliud accedat ex eo ductum quod ad se relatum fuisse Synodus ipsa testatur. Cum relatum, inquit, fuisset ad Synodum scripta quaedam, alia typis evulgata, alia manu exarata prodiisse, quae totam rationem peccati originalis sola corruptione hereditaria in omnibus hominibus inhaerente definiunt, et primi peccati Adae imputationem negant. Illis enim verbis aut exposita non est Placei sententia, aut male exposita est. Is enim primi peccati Adae imputationem nunquam simpliciter negavit, nunquam negatam voluit. Negavit tantum certam quandam peccati illius imputationem. Cum igitur imputationem primi illius peccati quandam affirmet, quandam neget, non exponitur eius sententia, si dicitur simpliciter et nulla distinctione adhibita primi peccati Adae imputationem negare.
english: Chapter Three. The same is proved by necessary arguments.

The arguments above, as I judge, were highly probable; the necessary ones follow. First: how could Placeus's judgment be condemned in a Synod in which it was neither proposed nor set forth? Yet it was not set forth in that National Synod which made that Decree. By whom would it have been set forth, if not by the one who accused it? If anyone did accuse it before the Synod, that man was D. Garissolius, the Synod's president. But how could he then have set it forth as it is — he who, even four years later, could not propose it as it is? Certainly in his explanation and defense of the Synodical Decree he attributes to Placeus a judgment Placeus does not own, and which openly clashes with the words in which Placeus had set out his mind — both in letters sent to Garissolius and in that manuscript which Garissolius later chose to call the later one — as I will make clearer than the midday sun in its place.

To this argument let another be added, drawn from what the Synod itself testifies was reported to it. When it had been reported, it says, to the Synod that certain writings had come forth — some published in type, others written by hand — which define the whole account of original sin by hereditary corruption alone inhering in all human beings, and deny the imputation of Adam's first sin. By those words Placeus's judgment is either not set forth, or is set forth badly. For he never simply denied the imputation of Adam's first sin, and never wished it denied. He denied only a certain kind of imputation of that sin. Since, therefore, he affirms one imputation of that first sin and denies another, his judgment is not set forth if he is said simply, and with no distinction applied, to deny the imputation of Adam's first sin.

source_text:
Tertium argumentum nobis suppeditat Synodi sententia damnatoria: Damnat Synodus doctrinam eiusmodi, quatenus peccati originalis naturam ad corruptionem hereditariam posterorum Adae ita restringit, ut imputationem excludat primi illius peccati quo lapsus est Adam. Illis enim verbis non damnat Synodus simpliciter eos, qui peccati originalis naturam ad corruptionem hereditariam restringunt; sed qui ita restringunt ut excludant imputationem primi illius peccati quo lapsus est Adam. Atqui Placeus nunquam peccati originalis naturam ad illam corruptionem ita restrinxit, ut imputationem excluderet primi illius peccati quo lapsus est Adam. Placeus igitur non est Synodi sententia damnatus.

Hoc confirmant verba quibus Clar. D. Garissolius in Epistola sua dedicatoria ad Ecclesiarum et Academiarum Tigurinae, Bernensis, Basileensis, Scaphusianae praesides sententiam Synodi expressit pag. 13. ait enim Synodi consultum factum esse, quo eorum sententia condemnatur, qui rationem originalis peccati in sola nativa corruptione ita constituunt, ut nullam primae Adami inobedientiae imputationem agnoscant. Atqui Placeus rationem originalis peccati in sola nativa corruptione non ita constituit, ut nullam primae Adami inobedientiae imputationem agnoscat: agnoscit enim aliquam. Cum igitur nullam agnoscere, et aliquam agnoscere, contradictorie opponantur, perspicuum est eo Synodi consulto Placei sententiam non esse damnatam.
english: A third argument is supplied to us by the Synod's condemning judgment: The Synod condemns doctrine of this kind insofar as it so restricts the nature of original sin to the hereditary corruption of Adam's posterity that it excludes the imputation of that first sin by which Adam fell. By those words the Synod does not simply condemn those who restrict the nature of original sin to hereditary corruption; it condemns those who so restrict it that they exclude the imputation of that first sin by which Adam fell. Yet Placeus never so restricted the nature of original sin to that corruption that he excluded the imputation of that first sin by which Adam fell. Placeus, therefore, is not condemned by the Synod's judgment.

This is confirmed by the words in which the distinguished D. Garissolius, in his dedicatory letter to the presidents of the churches and academies of Zurich, Bern, Basel, and Schaffhausen, expressed the Synod's judgment on page 13. He says the Synod's decree was made whereby the judgment of those is condemned who so set the account of original sin in native corruption alone that they acknowledge no imputation of Adam's first disobedience. Yet Placeus does not so constitute the account of original sin in native corruption alone that he acknowledges no imputation of Adam's first disobedience: for he acknowledges some. Since, therefore, to acknowledge none and to acknowledge some are contradictorily opposed, it is plain that by that Synod decree Placeus's judgment is not condemned.

source_text:
Idem etiam sonant verba Exscripti ex actis Synodi Montalbani habitae Octobri mense Ann. 1645. quod D. Garissolius libro suo praemisit. Perlectum est Decretum Synodi Nationalis Carentonensis, quo eorum doctrina damnatur, qui primum Adae peccatum docent posteris nequaquam imputari. Atqui Placeus non docet primum Adae peccatum posteris nequaquam imputari. Immo contra docet imputari, imputatione nimirum mediata seu consequente, quam ipse Dominus Garissolius fatetur se agnoscere. Doctrina igitur Placei non est eo Decreto damnata.

Hoc ipsum ex Synodi Nationalis testimonio colligi potest. Testatur enim omnes Ecclesias Protestantes et corruptionem illam, et imputationem hanc in omnes Adami posteros descendentem agnovisse. Id quod de illa imputatione primae Adami inobedientiae quam Placeus credit et docet, vere dicitur: de illa vero quam negat, non item. Unde enim sciri potest Ecclesiarum Protestantium sententia, nisi aut ex fidei confessionibus, aut ex decretis Synodicis, aut ex eorum libris quorum opera Deus usus est ad reformandam Ecclesiam suam? Atqui ex eiusmodi Confessionibus, Decretis, et libris nulla imputatio universaliter agnita colligi potest praeter eam unam, quam Placeus agnoscit. Hanc igitur unam qui negant, eos, non autem Placeum, Synodus damnat.

Praeterea Synodus omnes Pastores et Professores Imputationem hanc de qua loquitur negantes omnibus censuris subiiciendos censet, quo significat se talem imputationem intelligere, quae sit dogma religionis momentosum, et creditu necessarium. Id quod de imputatione quam Placeus negat vere dici non potest, sed de ea tantum quam ille probat et confitetur.

Denique Synodus non obscure innuit, illam imputationem primi Adae peccati, quam vult agnosci, tam aperte veram esse, ut probatione non egeat. Eo enim pertinere arbitror, quod eam nullo Scripturae testimonio, nulla ratione firmandam sibi censuit. Id autem in illam imputationem, quam Placeus agnoscit, competit; in eam vero quam negat, nullo modo. Quam enim illa necessario et evidenter vera videtur, tam ista diligenter inspicienti ne probabilis quidem apparet.
english: The same is also sounded by the words of the Extract from the acts of the Synod of Montauban held in the month of October in the year 1645, which D. Garissolius prefixed to his book. The Decree of the National Synod of Charenton was read, whereby the doctrine of those is condemned who teach that Adam's first sin is in no way imputed to posterity. Yet Placeus does not teach that Adam's first sin is in no way imputed to posterity. On the contrary, he teaches that it is imputed — namely by mediate or consequent imputation, which the same Lord Garissolius confesses that he himself acknowledges. Placeus's doctrine, therefore, is not condemned by that Decree.

This very point can be gathered from the National Synod's own testimony. For it testifies that all Protestant churches have acknowledged both that corruption and this imputation descending upon all Adam's posterity. That is truly said of that imputation of Adam's first disobedience which Placeus believes and teaches; of that which he denies, it is not. For from where can the judgment of the Protestant churches be known, if not from the confessions of faith, or from synodical decrees, or from the books of those whose labors God used to reform his Church? Yet from such Confessions, Decrees, and books no imputation universally acknowledged can be gathered except that one which Placeus acknowledges. Those, therefore, who deny that one — not Placeus — the Synod condemns.

Besides, the Synod judges that all pastors and professors who deny this imputation of which it speaks are to be subjected to all censures — whereby it signifies that it understands such an imputation to be a weighty dogma of religion, and necessary to be believed. That cannot truly be said of the imputation Placeus denies, but only of that which he proves and confesses.

Finally, the Synod not obscurely hints that that imputation of Adam's first sin which it wants acknowledged is so openly true that it does not need proof. For I judge it belongs to that point that the Synod thought it needed to be confirmed by no Scripture testimony and by no reason. That fits the imputation Placeus acknowledges; the one he denies, in no way. For as the former seems necessarily and evidently true, so the latter, to one who inspects carefully, does not even appear probable.

source_text:
CAPUT IV. Decretum Synodi, atque adeo Placei sententia, exponitur.

Sed ut res fiat clarior, nullusque in animo lectoris scrupulus haereat, Decretum paucis exponendum est, quidque revera Placeus sentiat aperiendum. Pendet autem id totum ex duabus distinctionibus, una primi Adae peccati, altera imputationis illius.

Et primum quidem Adae peccatum distingui potest in primum peccatum actuale, et primum peccatum habituale. Illud fuit actio inobedientiae Adami quae transiit; hoc fuit ab illa actione productum vitium, quod instar habitus in Adamo permansit, et ab eo una cum natura humana propagatum est in omnes eius posteros, uno Christo excepto. Hoc vitium vere peccatum esse omnes, quicunque Pelagiani non sunt, agnoscunt. Imputari etiam Adae posteris, et damnandi vim habere, nisi condonetur, omnes Ecclesiae Protestantes hactenus summo consensu crediderunt, ut ex eorum patet Confessionibus. Itaque si de huius primi Adae peccati imputatione Decretum Synodi accipitur, id pro verissimo aequissimoque habet Placeus, meritoque damnatam eorum doctrinam censet, qui hoc quidem peccatum se agnoscere profitentur, nulli tamen imputari, quantumvis infideli, contendunt. Esse enim hoc seculo qui id doceant, et quidem editis libris, testis est Doctiss. V. Walaeus Theologiae Lugduni Batavorum dum viveret Professor, Epist. antep. ad Henricum Flokenium Bremam scripta.

Sin vero per primum Adae peccatum, primum eius peccatum actuale intelligitur — id quod mihi verisimilius videtur: nam et illud omnium absolute primum fuit, et eo magis proprie lapsus esse Adam dicitur, quam primo suo peccato habituali — distinguenda est imputatio in Imputationem immediatam seu antecedentem, et imputationem mediatam seu consequentem. Illa fit immediate, hoc est, non mediante corruptione; haec fit mediate, hoc est, mediante corruptione haereditaria. Illa ordine naturae corruptionem antecedit; haec sequitur. Illa corruptionis causa censetur esse, haec effectus. Illam Placeus reicit; hanc admittit.
english: Chapter Four. The Synod's Decree, and so Placeus's judgment, is set forth.

But so that the matter may become clearer, and no scruple may stick in the reader's mind, the Decree must be set forth in a few words, and what Placeus really thinks must be opened. The whole hangs on two distinctions: one of Adam's first sin, the other of its imputation.

And first, Adam's sin can be distinguished into first actual sin and first habitual sin. The former was Adam's act of disobedience, which passed away; the latter was the vice produced from that act, which remained in Adam after the manner of a habit, and was propagated from him, together with human nature, into all his posterity, Christ alone excepted. That this vice is truly sin, all who are not Pelagians acknowledge. That it is also imputed to Adam's posterity, and has the force of condemning unless it is forgiven, all the Protestant churches have hitherto believed with the highest consensus, as is plain from their Confessions. Therefore if the Synod's Decree is taken of the imputation of this first sin of Adam, Placeus holds it for most true and most equitable, and rightly judges the doctrine of those condemned who profess that they acknowledge this sin, yet contend that it is imputed to no one, however unbelieving. That there are those in this age who teach that, and even in published books, the most learned V. Walaeus, while he lived Professor of Theology at Leiden, is witness — in the letter prefixed to his work, written to Heinrich Flocken of Bremen.

But if by Adam's first sin his first actual sin is understood — which seems to me more likely: for that was absolutely first of all, and Adam is more properly said to have fallen by it than by his first habitual sin — then imputation must be distinguished into immediate or antecedent imputation, and mediate or consequent imputation. The former happens immediately — that is, not through the mediation of corruption; the latter happens mediately — that is, through hereditary corruption. The former precedes corruption in the order of nature; the latter follows. The former is held to be the cause of corruption; the latter its effect. Placeus rejects the former; he admits the latter.

Quaeritur nunc an fuerit eius sententia Synodi Decreto damnata? Si damnata est, ideo damnata est, vel quia utramque illam imputationem coniunctim non admittit, vel quia imputationem immediatam seu antecedentem reicit. Primum dici non potest. Coniunctim enim admitti non possunt absque contradictionis implicatione. Nam qui dicit primum peccatum actuale Adami eius posteris imputari immediate, is negat imputari mediate: idem enim immediate significat ac non mediate. Imputari igitur immediate, et imputari non mediante corruptione, idem plane sunt. Qui igitur affirmaret simul imputari primum illud peccatum immediate et mediate, is simul et negaret mediante corruptione imputari et affirmaret, seseque adeo contradictione implicaret. Id quod sine dubio a nobis exigere Synodus noluit. Taceo non esse aequitati consentaneum, ut idem numero peccatum eidem bis imputetur, semel ante corruptionem haereditariam, et iterum post illam corruptionem. Una certe imputatio sufficit.

Quandoquidem igitur ambae illae imputationes simul retineri nequeunt, alteraque eligenda est repudiata altera, vel Synodus in dubio reliquit quam intellexerit, mediatam an immediatam; vel id non reliquit in dubio. Si prius: etiam in dubio reliquit, utrum Placei sententiam Decreto suo condemnaverit, necne. Quare decet illius Lectores suum de Placeo iudicium suspendere, neque eum magis damnatum, quam indemnatum, putare.

Sin est aliquid in Decreto quod imputationem determinet. Si damnatur eorum doctrina qui negant imputationem mediatam, non damnatur Placei doctrina: is enim imputationem mediatam agnoscit. Si damnatur eorum doctrina qui negant imputationem immediatam, damnatur quidem Placei doctrina — sed non damnatur sola, damnaretur enim cum ea ipsis Apostoli Pauli doctrina, et virorum maximi nominis.
english: It is asked now whether his judgment was condemned by the Synod's Decree. If it was condemned, it was condemned either because he does not admit both those imputations jointly, or because he rejects immediate or antecedent imputation. The first cannot be said. For they cannot be admitted jointly without involving a contradiction. For whoever says that Adam's first actual sin is imputed to his posterity immediately denies that it is imputed mediately: for immediately means the same as not mediately. To be imputed immediately, and to be imputed not through the mediation of corruption, are plainly the same. Whoever, therefore, would affirm that that first sin is imputed at once immediately and mediately would at once both deny and affirm that it is imputed through corruption — and would so involve himself in contradiction. That, without doubt, the Synod did not wish to require of us. I pass over in silence that it is not agreeable to equity that the same numerical sin be imputed twice to the same person — once before hereditary corruption, and again after that corruption. One imputation certainly suffices.

Since, therefore, those two imputations cannot be retained together, and one must be chosen with the other repudiated, either the Synod left in doubt which it understood — the mediate or the immediate — or it did not leave that in doubt. If the former: it also left in doubt whether it condemned Placeus's judgment by its Decree, or not. Wherefore it is fitting that its readers suspend their judgment concerning Placeus, and not think him more condemned than uncondemned.

But if there is something in the Decree that determines the imputation: if the doctrine of those who deny mediate imputation is condemned, Placeus's doctrine is not condemned — for he acknowledges mediate imputation. If the doctrine of those who deny immediate imputation is condemned, Placeus's doctrine is indeed condemned — but it is not condemned alone, for with it the doctrine of the Apostle Paul himself, and of men of the greatest name, would be condemned.

source_text:
Videbiturque tibi, lector, testis idoneus Aegidius Hunnius Augustanae Confessionis Theologus celebris? En eius testimonium Art. de peccat.: Ostendit ergo Apostolus Paulus lapsum Adami NON IMMEDIATE propter se, sed MEDIATE et propter aliud nobis eius posteris IMPUTARI, quia videlicet per lapsum istum polluta est natura primorum parentum, ut non nisi peccato corruptos et vitiatos liberos procreare possent. Quod si enim Adamus tum ad imaginem Dei integer eiusmodi posteris potuisset, ut in posteros non vitium proprium derivaretur a primis parentibus, tum lapsus ille, tanquam peccatum alienum, eis plane non imputaretur. Palam igitur ostendit Paulus non illud delictum nobis ad condemnationem pervenire NISI MEDIATE, quatenus per delictum illud invehitur in naturam horribilis corruptio, quam per generationem propagavit in ipsas posteritates. Habes in eo distinctionem imputationis primi peccati actualis Adae in mediatam et immediatam, illa assertam, hac reiectam, eamque doctrinam Apostolum Paulum palam docuisse.

Sed fortasse aliter sentiebant Ecclesiae Protestantes. Audi igitur etiam Calvinum Comment. in Rom. cap. 5. vers. 15.: Quod unius delicto multi periisse tradit, non sic accipies quasi extra culpam ipsi essemus: sed quia eius peccatum peccati nostri causa est, exitium nostrum ei Paulus adscribit. Peccatum nostrum voco, quod nobis ingenitum est et cum quo nascimur. Alia Calvini loca hic non proferam; quid enim ille senserit, testem habeo locupletem D. Garissolium, De Imp. primi pecc. cap. IX. §. XI. pag. 299.: Quantumvis, inquit, lapsus primi reatus ad nos NON perveniat NISI MEDIANTE CORRUPTIONE, QUOD CUM CALVINO AGNOSCIMUS, et superius expositum est, illud tamen obstare non potest, quominus reatus ille sit non tantum corruptionis nostrae, sed et primi actualis Adae peccati reatus: nempe illius, est immediate, huius mediate. Haec est ipsissima Placei sententia; quae si damnata est, etiam Apostoli Pauli, etiam Aegidii Hunnii et Calvini, immo ipsius D. Garissolii — si suam ipse sententiam verbis illis fideliter expressit — doctrina damnata est.

Idem D. Garissolius eodem lib. cap. VIII. §. III. pag. 206. testatur imputationem de qua agitur Rom. 5. necessario cum corruptione nativa coniungi, imo EAM SEQUI. Si eam sequitur, imputatio est consequens seu mediata, quam cum Apostolo Placeus docet. Addam hic quoque testimonium Petri Martyris, Loc. Com. De pec. orig. §. 34., et doctissimi Walaei, Resp. ad Cens. Corv. cap. VIII. pag. 238.: Reatus primi peccati ad condemnationem, ut Apostolus loquitur, Rom. 5.16., nullo modo posteris IMPUTARI POTEST NISI MEDIANTE illius peccati inhaerenti vitiositate.

Si igitur damnasset Synodus Placei doctrinam, haberet ille quidem solatium miserorum, consortesque huiusce condemnationis viros maximos; sed profecto eam, uti iam multis argumentis probavi, non condemnavit. Si suo illo Decreto eorum doctrinam Synodus damnasset, qui negant imputationem immediatam seu antecedentem, eadem utique damnasset absolute eorum doctrinam, qui peccati originalis naturam ad corruptionem haereditariam posterorum Adae restringunt. Atqui Synodus non simpliciter damnavit doctrinam, quae peccati originalis naturam ad corruptionem haereditariam restringit, sed quae ita restringit, ut imputationem excludat primi illius peccati quo lapsus est Adam. Ergo Synodus eorum doctrinam non damnavit, qui negant imputationem immediatam. Sola imputatio mediata seu consequens cum illa restrictione potest consistere: eam igitur solam Synodus intellexit.

Itaque ea prudentia Decretum suum contexuit, ut cum ter corruptionis ac imputationis meminerit, perpetuo prius corruptionem quam imputationem nominaverit — ut insinuaret imputationem sequentem, non antecedentem. Denique Decretum Synodi, aut congruit cum S. Scriptura, aut non. Si non, Art. V. Conf. Fid. obstat. Si congruit, non damnat eorum doctrinam qui, retenta imputatione mediata, solam immediatam negant. Ut sit finis, ipse D. Garissolius hanc imputationis distinctionem probavit, eaque bene intellecta controversiam finiri posse putavit. Distinctio sic intellecta consensum stabiliri non posset, si Decreto damnata esset doctrina quae admissa imputatione mediata negat immediatam. Non est igitur existimandum eo Decreto doctrinam illam esse damnatam.
english: And will Aegidius Hunnius, the celebrated theologian of the Augsburg Confession, seem to you, reader, a fit witness? Here is his testimony in the Article on sin: The Apostle Paul therefore shows that Adam's fall is imputed to us his posterity NOT IMMEDIATELY for its own sake, but MEDIATELY and on account of another thing — because, namely, by that fall the nature of the first parents was polluted, so that they could beget children only corrupted and vitiated by sin. For if Adam, then upright in the image of God, could have had such posterity that no proper vice was derived into posterity from the first parents, then that fall, as another's sin, would plainly not be imputed to them. Paul therefore openly shows that that offense does not reach us for condemnation EXCEPT MEDIATELY, insofar as through that offense a horrible corruption is brought into nature, which he propagated by generation into the posterities themselves. Could that be declared more clearly or more expressly? You have in him the distinction of the imputation of Adam's first actual sin into mediate and immediate — the former asserted, the latter rejected — and that the Apostle Paul openly taught that doctrine.

But perhaps the Protestant churches thought otherwise. Hear, then, also Calvin in his Commentary on Romans 5:15 (Romans 5:15): When he teaches that many perished by one man's offense, you will not take it as if we ourselves were outside fault; but because his sin is the cause of our sin, Paul ascribes our ruin to him. I call our sin that which is inborn in us and with which we are born. I will not bring forward other places of Calvin here; for what he thought, I have a rich witness in D. Garissolius, On the Imputation of the First Sin, chapter 9, section 11, page 299: However much, he says, the guilt of the first lapse does NOT reach us EXCEPT THROUGH THE MEDIATION OF CORRUPTION — WHICH WE ACKNOWLEDGE WITH CALVIN, and which was set forth above — that still cannot hinder that guilt from being not only the guilt of our corruption, but also the guilt of Adam's first actual sin: namely, of the former immediately, of the latter mediately. This is Placeus's very judgment; which, if it is condemned, then the doctrine of the Apostle Paul also, of Aegidius Hunnius and of Calvin, and even of D. Garissolius himself — if he faithfully expressed his own judgment in those words — is condemned.

The same D. Garissolius in the same book, chapter 8, section 3, page 206, testifies that the imputation treated in Romans 5 is necessarily joined with native corruption, and even FOLLOWS IT. If it follows it, the imputation is consequent or mediate, which Placeus teaches with the Apostle. I will add here also the testimony of Peter Martyr, Common Places, On Original Sin, section 34, and of the most learned Walaeus, Reply to the Censure of Corvinus, chapter 8, page 238: The guilt of the first sin unto condemnation, as the Apostle speaks in Romans 5:16, CAN IN NO WAY BE IMPUTED to posterity EXCEPT THROUGH the inherent viciousness of that sin.

If, therefore, the Synod had condemned Placeus's doctrine, he would indeed have the comfort of the miserable, and men of the greatest name as partners in this condemnation; but in fact, as I have already proved by many arguments, it did not condemn it. If by that Decree the Synod had condemned the doctrine of those who deny immediate or antecedent imputation, it would certainly also have condemned absolutely the doctrine of those who restrict the nature of original sin to the hereditary corruption of Adam's posterity. Yet the Synod did not simply condemn the doctrine which restricts the nature of original sin to hereditary corruption, but that which so restricts it that it excludes the imputation of that first sin by which Adam fell. Therefore the Synod did not condemn the doctrine of those who deny immediate imputation. Only mediate or consequent imputation can stand with that restriction: that alone, therefore, the Synod understood.

And so with that prudence it wove its Decree, that when it thrice remembered corruption and imputation, it always named corruption before imputation — to hint that the imputation to be understood is the one that follows, not the one that precedes, that hereditary corruption. Finally, the Synod's Decree either agrees with Holy Scripture or it does not. If it does not, Article V of the Confession of Faith, which that very Synod approved, stands in the way of receiving it. If it agrees, then certainly it does not condemn the doctrine of those who, keeping the mediate imputation of Adam's first sin, deny only the immediate or antecedent. To make an end: D. Garissolius himself, than whom no one was less fair to Placeus, approved this distinction of imputation, and thought that once it was well understood the controversy could be finished. Yet with the distinction so understood, consensus could in no way be established if by that Synodical Decree the doctrine had been condemned which, admitting mediate imputation of that act, denies the immediate. There would remain a perfect disagreement between that Decree and Placeus's judgment. It is not, therefore, to be thought that by that Decree that doctrine was condemned.

Praecesserant enim in Manuscripto illo, quod D. Garissolius Posterius appellat, haec verba. Est igitur quaestio inter nos instituta dumtaxat de primo peccato Adami sumpto primo modo, hoc est de actuali eius inobedientia, de actione illa interna et externa, qua Dei legem transgressus est Adam, praecisa ab habituali corruptione, quae actionem illam secuta est: an ea nobis nascentibus imputetur? Huic quaestioni nondum negatione simplici, sed distinctione rursus satisfaciendum videtur. Est enim animo concipi duplex imputatio, Immediata et mediata (vel, ut idem aliis verbis dicam) Antecedens et Consequens. Potuitne Placeus apertius significare, se distinctionem illam imputationis de actione illa, qua primum Adamus reum se fecit, intelligere? Deinde subiiciebatur, Imputationem immediatam esse eam, qua putatur actio illa Adami, hoc est, vetiti fructus manducatio, eius posteris omnibus (Christo excepto) proxime, immediate, hoc ipso quod filii sunt Adami, imputari ad duas poenas proprie dictas, privationem iustitiae originalis, et mortem aeternam. Iam autem de quo unum distinctionis membrum intelligitur, de eodem intelligi debet alterum; alioqui non esset distinctio; non enim unum quid distingueretur. Denique subiungebat Placeus Imputationem mediatam esse eam, quae sit mediante corruptione haereditaria. Cuius autem, quaeso, peccati imputatio fieri potest mediante illa corruptione, nisi peccati actualis Adami, quod corruptionem illam peperit? Addebat etiam hanc rationem: Huius enim corruptionis participatione communicamus peccato Adami, eique, ut ita loquar, habitualiter consentimus. Quibus verbis aperte distinguebat peccatum Adami ab illa corruptione. Itaque non ipsam corruptionem intelligebat per peccatum Adami, sed actualem inobedientiam, unde illa fluxit.

Hanc autem Placei rationem D. Garissolius approbavit et commendavit, ac etiam retorfit. Sed in quem, nescio; in Placeum enim non potuit, ut iam patet. Si quis autem alius Placeo notus imputationem actualis peccati Adae negavit et refutavit, id de imputatione immediata seu antecedente sola accipi debet, non de mediata seu consequente, quam neque vult negatam, neque etiam eius argumenta oppugnant.
english: For in that Manuscript which D. Garissolius calls the Later, these words had gone before. The question set on foot between us is only about Adam's first sin taken in the first way — that is, about his actual disobedience, about that inward and outward act by which Adam transgressed God's law, cut off from the habitual corruption that followed that act: whether that is imputed to us when we are born. To this question it seems a bare negation does not yet answer; a distinction must again satisfy. For the mind can conceive a double imputation — Immediate and mediate (or, to say the same in other words, Antecedent and Consequent). Could Placeus more openly signify that he understands that distinction of imputation of that act by which Adam first made himself guilty? Next it was added that immediate imputation is that by which that act of Adam — that is, the eating of the forbidden fruit — is thought to be imputed to all his posterity (Christ excepted) proximately, immediately, by this very fact that they are sons of Adam, unto two penalties properly so called: the privation of original righteousness, and eternal death. But of that about which one member of the distinction is understood, the other ought to be understood as well; otherwise there would be no distinction; for one thing would not be distinguished. Finally Placeus added that mediate imputation is that which takes place through hereditary corruption. And of what sin, I ask, can imputation be made through that corruption, unless of Adam's actual sin, which produced that corruption? He also added this reason: For by participation in this corruption we communicate in Adam's sin, and, so to speak, habitually consent to it. By which words he openly distinguished Adam's sin from that corruption. Therefore he did not understand the corruption itself by Adam's sin, but the actual disobedience from which it flowed.

This reason of Placeus D. Garissolius approved and recommended, and even turned back. But upon whom, I do not know; for upon Placeus he could not, as is already plain. But if anyone else known to Placeus denied and refuted the imputation of Adam's actual sin, that must be taken of immediate or antecedent imputation alone, not of the mediate or consequent, which he neither wants denied, nor do his arguments attack.
